description: Bhaktapur, Khwopa in Newar, is the best-preserved of the valley's three royal cities. Its Durbar Square, Taumadhi Square and Tachupal Square hold the five-roofed Nyatapola, the Palace of Fifty-Five Windows and the Golden Gate, and the municipality reinvests visitor fees in conservation and in living festivals such as Bisket Jatra.

loreChunks.title: Bhupatindra's Masterpiece
loreChunks.text: Nyatapola, whose name means 'five-storeyed' in Newar, was built in 1702 by King Bhupatindra Malla of Bhaktapur, the most ambitious builder among the city's rulers. Rising about thirty metres, it is the tallest pagoda in Nepal and dominates Taumadhi Square. Bhupatindra reigned from 1696 to 1722, a period when Bhaktapur, though smaller than Kathmandu and Patan, rivalled them in artistic splendour. Local tradition tells that the king built Nyatapola to house a powerful goddess who could calm the fierce Bhairav, whose temple next door was believed to be causing trouble in the city. The construction became a communal effort, and stories describe the king himself carrying bricks to inspire the townspeople. Completed in a remarkably short time, the temple became a symbol of Bhaktapur's pride and has remained the city's emblem for more than three centuries.

loreChunks.title: Five Roofs on Five Stages
loreChunks.text: Nyatapola achieves its soaring height through a combination of a tall five-stage plinth and five diminishing roofs. A steep stone stairway climbs the plinth's central axis on the main side, flanked on each stage by pairs of stone guardians. The temple's brick walls, timber struts and tiled roofs follow the classic Newar pagoda form, but the proportions are taller and more slender than usual, and the engineering is remarkably robust. The temple survived the great earthquake of 1934, which devastated Bhaktapur, and the 2015 earthquake with only minor damage, a testament to its builders' skill. The carved struts supporting each roof depict forms of the goddess and attendant deities. From the top of the plinth visitors gain sweeping views over Taumadhi Square and the roofs of the old city, a fine reward for the steep climb.

loreChunks.title: Guardians Ten Times Stronger
loreChunks.text: The stone guardians lining Nyatapola's stairway are among the most famous sculptures in Nepal. At the bottom stand the legendary wrestlers Jayamal and Phattu, said to have possessed the strength of ten ordinary men. Above them stand elephants, each said to be ten times stronger than the wrestlers, then lions, then griffin-like sardulas, and finally the goddesses Baghini and Singhini, the tiger and lion goddesses, each pair ten times stronger than the one below. The sequence expresses a hierarchy of power that culminates in the deity inside: Siddhi Lakshmi, a Tantric goddess of great power, whose image is hidden from public view and served only by priests. The guardians therefore lead the eye and the spirit upward, from human strength to animal, mythical and divine power, reminding every visitor who climbs the steps of the goddess's supremacy.

loreChunks.title: The Hidden Goddess of Taumadhi
loreChunks.text: Unlike the neighbouring Bhairavnath temple, which plays a central role in Bhaktapur's Bisket Jatra festival, Nyatapola is relatively quiet ritually. Its goddess, Siddhi Lakshmi, is worshipped privately by priests, and the sanctum is closed to the public. Yet the temple's presence shapes the life of Taumadhi Square, where residents meet, children play and festivals unfold. During Bisket Jatra in April, the giant chariot of Bhairav is pulled through the square beneath Nyatapola, and crowds climb the temple's plinth to watch the tug-of-war between the upper and lower halves of the city. The legend that the goddess was installed to restrain Bhairav adds drama to this scene, as the two deities face each other across the square. Visitors may climb the plinth steps, but should not attempt to enter the sanctum or disturb the priests.

loreChunks.title: Standing Through Two Great Earthquakes
loreChunks.text: Nyatapola's endurance through the earthquakes of 1934 and 2015, both of which caused widespread destruction in Bhaktapur, has made it a symbol of resilience. Engineers and historians have studied the temple to understand its stability, pointing to its broad stepped plinth, well-bonded brickwork and carefully designed timber framework. After 2015 the temple required only modest repairs, while many buildings around Taumadhi Square needed extensive reconstruction. Conservation focuses on maintaining the roofs to prevent water damage to the timber, conserving the carved struts and monitoring the stone guardians for weathering. Bhaktapur Municipality, which manages the city's heritage and collects visitor fees, plays a major role in this work alongside the Department of Archaeology. The city's model of reinvesting tourism revenue in conservation is often cited as one of the most successful in the valley.

audioHook.script: Climb the steep stone stairway of Nyatapola, and you will pass a staircase of guardians. At the bottom stand two legendary wrestlers, each as strong as ten men. Above them, elephants, ten times stronger. Then lions, then mythical griffins, and at the very top two goddesses, the strongest of all. And inside, hidden from every visitor, sits a Tantric goddess more powerful than them all. King Bhupatindra Malla built this five-roofed temple in 1702, and at about thirty metres it is the tallest pagoda in Nepal. It survived the great earthquakes of 1934 and 2015 almost untouched. Legend says he built it to tame the fierce Bhairav next door. Did it work? Book a verified local storyteller nearby and let a guide tell you the rivalry of Taumadhi Square.

loreChunks.title: A Palace Rebuilt by a Builder King
loreChunks.text: The Palace of Fifty-Five Windows was the residence of the Malla kings of Bhaktapur. Its origins go back to the fifteenth century, when King Yaksha Malla ruled a unified valley from Bhaktapur, but its present form owes most to King Bhupatindra Malla, who remodelled it at the end of the seventeenth century. Bhupatindra, who also built Nyatapola, was passionate about art and architecture, and he transformed his palace into a showcase of Newar woodcarving. After Bhaktapur fell to Prithvi Narayan Shah in 1769, the palace lost its royal function, and it suffered severe damage in the 1934 earthquake, after which parts were rebuilt with less care. Today it houses parts of the National Art Gallery and forms the centrepiece of Bhaktapur Durbar Square, a reminder of the days when Bhaktapur was one of three rival royal capitals in the valley.

loreChunks.title: Fifty-Five Windows in a Row
loreChunks.text: The palace's name comes from the long row of carved wooden windows that runs along its upper floor, a single continuous band of lattice and frames that gives the facade its distinctive rhythm. Each window is a masterpiece of Newar joinery, with interlocking lattices that admit light and air while preserving privacy, and frames carved with deities, animals and floral patterns. The windows overhang the brick facade below, supported by carved struts, and their dark timber contrasts with the warm red of the brickwork. The palace originally included many courtyards, of which only a few survive. Adjoining wings, rebuilt after 1934 in a whitewashed style, show the change in building taste over the twentieth century. Standing in front of the palace, visitors can see how the windows create a continuity that ties the whole facade together.

loreChunks.title: Windows as Sacred Frames
loreChunks.text: In Newar architecture, windows are more than openings. Their carved frames often include images of deities, protective figures and auspicious symbols such as peacocks, makaras and lotuses, turning each window into a small shrine. The windows of the palace allowed the king and his family to observe festivals and processions in the square while remaining hidden behind the lattices, a reminder of the separation between royalty and subjects. At the same time, the windows presented a decorated face to the city, signalling the king's wealth and piety. Inside, palace rooms were decorated with paintings of deities and royal portraits. The carved figures on the windows reward close attention, and visitors with binoculars or zoom lenses can pick out details that most passers-by miss, including tiny figures of musicians, dancers and animals tucked into the frames.

loreChunks.title: Festivals Before the Palace
loreChunks.text: The palace faced the square where Bhaktapur's great festivals unfolded, and the king watched from its windows as masked dances, processions and chariots passed below. During Dashain, the palace's Taleju shrine became the focus of royal ritual, and during other festivals the square filled with music and celebration. Bhaktapur is renowned for its living traditions, including the Navadurga masked dances performed by hereditary groups, and many of these performances still take place in the city's squares. Although the palace no longer houses a king, its presence continues to frame the ritual life of the city. Visitors who come during festivals can see how the square fills with people and how the palace forms the backdrop to events celebrated in much the same way for centuries. Bhaktapur's festival calendar is among the richest in the whole valley.

loreChunks.title: Damage in 1934 and 2015
loreChunks.text: The palace suffered severe damage in the 1934 earthquake, which destroyed much of Bhaktapur, and some of its rebuilt wings lack the craftsmanship of the original. The 2015 earthquake caused further damage, including cracks in the walls and damage to the carved windows. Restoration has been carried out by the Department of Archaeology and Bhaktapur Municipality, with traditional craftsmen repairing the timber and brickwork. Conservation of the windows is particularly demanding, as each lattice and frame must be repaired or replaced by hand using matching wood and joinery. Bhaktapur's long history of heritage conservation, including the German-supported Bhaktapur Development Project of the 1970s and 1980s, has helped to maintain local craft skills. Visitors can help by respecting barriers around restoration areas and by paying the city entry fee, which funds conservation work across Bhaktapur.

audioHook.script: Stand back and count the windows on the upper floor of this long brick palace. There should be fifty-five, carved in a single unbroken row. This was the home of Bhaktapur's Malla kings, remodelled at the end of the seventeenth century by King Bhupatindra Malla, the same builder king who raised Nyatapola. From behind those lattices, the royal family watched festivals in the square without being seen. Look closely at a single frame, and you may find tiny musicians, dancers and peacocks hidden in the carving. The great earthquake of 1934 shattered much of this palace, and parts were rebuilt in a plainer style. Can you spot where old meets new? loreChunks.title: A Stone Temple for the Mother Goddess
loreChunks.text: Vatsala Durga is a stone shikhara temple in Bhaktapur Durbar Square, built in 1672 by King Jagat Prakash Malla and dedicated to Vatsala, a form of the mother goddess Durga. Its style follows the north Indian shikhara tradition that had become fashionable in the valley after Patan's Krishna Mandir, and it represents Bhaktapur's response to the stone temples of its rival cities. Beside it stands a great bell, hung in 1737 by King Ranajit Malla, the last Malla king of Bhaktapur, to accompany the worship of Taleju. The temple and bell together formed part of the royal ritual landscape in front of the palace. Ranajit Malla lost his kingdom to Prithvi Narayan Shah in 1769, but the bell he donated remains, and it still sounds over the square during the worship of the royal goddess.

loreChunks.title: Shikhara and Pavilion
loreChunks.text: Vatsala Durga rises on a stepped plinth in the form of a stone shikhara, a tapering tower surrounded at its base by small pavilions and pinnacles. The design echoes the Krishna Mandir in Patan but on a smaller scale, and its carved stone details show the skill of Bhaktapur's craftsmen. Stone animal figures guard the stairway, and the tower is crowned with a gilded finial. The temple's slender silhouette contrasts with the broad brick pagodas around it. The neighbouring bell is suspended from a frame on its own plinth, and its large bronze body carries an inscription recording its donation. Together the shikhara and the bell occupy a prominent place in front of the palace, framing the view of the Fifty-Five Window Palace for visitors who enter the square from the west and pause here before exploring further.

loreChunks.title: The Bell of Barking Dogs
loreChunks.text: The bell beside Vatsala Durga is famous as the 'bell of barking dogs'. According to local tradition, whenever the bell is rung, dogs in the square begin to bark and whine, and residents often say the sound disturbs them. Some explain the phenomenon by the bell's pitch; others link it with folklore about spirits and the goddess. The bell was originally rung to accompany the daily worship of Taleju and, according to some accounts, to signal a curfew in the city. Vatsala Durga herself is a form of the mother goddess, protector of children and of the city, and her image inside the sanctum is honoured by priests and devotees. The combination of a stone temple to the goddess and a bell whose sound affects animals makes this one of the most memorable spots in Bhaktapur for visitors of every age.

loreChunks.title: Worship of the Mother Goddess
loreChunks.text: Vatsala Durga receives daily worship, and her shrine is particularly important during Dashain, the great festival of Durga, when the goddess's victory over the buffalo demon Mahishasura is celebrated. During this festival Bhaktapur's squares fill with worshippers, and the royal goddess Taleju receives special rituals in the palace. The bell beside the temple is rung during worship, its distinctive sound carrying across the square. Bhaktapur's residents also honour Vatsala Durga during smaller festivals and on auspicious days of the lunar calendar. The temple's position near the western entrance to the square means that it is one of the first monuments visitors encounter, and its steps provide a good vantage point for watching the life of the square. Visitors should never ring the bell, which is reserved for ritual use by the temple's priests and attendants.

loreChunks.title: Collapse and Rebuilding
loreChunks.text: Vatsala Durga collapsed in the 2015 earthquake, its stone tower falling into a heap of masonry, and its loss was one of the most visible signs of the earthquake's impact on Bhaktapur Durbar Square. The bell beside it survived. Reconstruction began after careful documentation of the fallen stones, many of which were recovered, numbered and reused. The rebuilding was carried out with traditional techniques together with structural improvements intended to increase the tower's earthquake resistance. The temple had also been damaged in the 1934 earthquake and rebuilt at that time. Its rebuilding after 2015 restored the familiar silhouette to the square. Visitors comparing photographs from before 2015 with the present temple can see how closely the rebuilt tower follows its predecessor, and a guide can explain the techniques used to reassemble the stone.

audioHook.script: Next to this slender stone temple hangs a big bronze bell with a strange reputation. People in Bhaktapur call it the bell of barking dogs, because whenever it rings, the dogs of the square start barking and whining. King Ranajit Malla, the last Malla king of Bhaktapur, hung it in 1737 to accompany the worship of the royal goddess. The temple beside it, Vatsala Durga, was built in 1672 for a form of the mother goddess Durga. In the 2015 earthquake the stone tower crashed to the ground, while the bell held on. The tower you see is rebuilt, many stones back in their original places. Why do the dogs react? Book a verified local storyteller nearby and let a guide tell you what Bhaktapur believes.

loreChunks.title: From One Roof to Three
loreChunks.text: The Bhairavnath temple stands on Taumadhi Square beside Nyatapola. It began as a one-storey temple, and in 1717 King Bhupatindra Malla raised it to its present three-tiered form. The temple is dedicated to Bhairav, the fierce form of Shiva, who in Bhaktapur is worshipped as Kasi Bishwanath, a name that links him with the sacred city of Varanasi. Local legend tells that Bhairav came to Bhaktapur from Varanasi to watch the Bisket Jatra festival, disguised as an ordinary man. A tantric recognised him and tried to capture him; Bhairav sank into the earth, but the tantric cut off his head, which remained in Bhaktapur. This story explains why Bhairav is worshipped here as a head. The temple was badly damaged in the 1934 earthquake and rebuilt, and it remains the focus of the city's most important festival.

loreChunks.title: A Rectangular Pagoda
loreChunks.text: Bhairavnath is a rectangular pagoda with three tiers, a less common form than the square plan used for most Newar temples. Its broad facade faces Taumadhi Square, and a small niche on the front holds a gilded image of Bhairav's head, through which offerings are made, since the main sanctum is entered from the rear. The roofs are supported by carved struts and decorated with metal ornaments, and the eaves are hung with bells. Beside the temple, the huge wooden wheels and parts of Bhairav's chariot for Bisket Jatra are stored between festivals, a reminder of the temple's ritual role. The contrast between Bhairavnath's broad, horizontal mass and Nyatapola's soaring verticality creates the distinctive composition of Taumadhi Square, one of the most photographed urban spaces in Nepal and a favourite of painters for generations.

loreChunks.title: The Head of Bhairav
loreChunks.text: Bhairav's worship as a head only is one of Bhaktapur's most distinctive religious features. The gilded head in the niche on the facade is the public focus of devotion, and devotees push offerings through a small opening below it. Bhairav is understood in Bhaktapur as a powerful protector of the city, and his fierce nature is balanced by the goddess Siddhi Lakshmi in neighbouring Nyatapola, according to the legend that Bhupatindra Malla built the five-roofed temple to restrain him. The temple's carvings include forms of Bhairav and other deities associated with Shiva. During Bisket Jatra, Bhairav is carried in his chariot, and his union with his consort Bhadrakali is celebrated as part of the New Year festival. The head of Bhairav thus stands at the centre of a rich web of myth that links Bhaktapur with Varanasi and the gods.

loreChunks.title: Bisket Jatra
loreChunks.text: Bisket Jatra, Bhaktapur's New Year festival held in mid-April, is one of the most spectacular events in the valley. Bhairav's three-tiered chariot, carrying the god's image, is pulled through the streets around Taumadhi Square, and the city's upper and lower halves compete in a tug-of-war to pull it toward their own neighbourhoods. The winning side is believed to enjoy good fortune for the coming year. The festival also includes the raising of a tall wooden pole, the lingo, and its felling on New Year's Day, which local legend links with the defeat of serpent demons. Crowds pack the square, climbing temple plinths and rooftops for a view. Visitors who attend should be aware that the tug-of-war can be rough and dangerous, and should follow local guidance, watching from a safe position rather than joining the crowd at the ropes.

loreChunks.title: Rebuilt After 1934, Repaired After 2015
loreChunks.text: Bhairavnath was severely damaged in the 1934 earthquake and rebuilt, and the 2015 earthquake caused further damage to its roofs and walls. Repairs were carried out by Bhaktapur Municipality and the Department of Archaeology using traditional materials and techniques. The temple's role in Bisket Jatra means that conservation must also consider the impact of the festival, when crowds and the chariot pass close by. The chariot itself, assembled and repaired each year from wood, is part of the city's living heritage and requires skilled carpenters who follow traditional designs. Bhaktapur's approach to conservation, combining physical repair with support for festivals and crafts, has helped the city retain its distinctive character. The Bhaktapur entry fee funds much of this work, so visitors' contributions directly support the maintenance of temples like Bhairavnath.

audioHook.script: The broad three-roofed temple beside Nyatapola belongs to Bhairav, and here he is worshipped as a head only. Look for the small golden face in the niche on the front. Legend says Bhairav came from the holy city of Varanasi to watch Bhaktapur's New Year festival in disguise. A tantric recognised him, and as the god sank into the earth to escape, the tantric cut off his head, which stayed here forever. King Bhupatindra Malla raised this temple to three roofs in 1717, and legend says he built Nyatapola next door with a goddess strong enough to keep Bhairav in check. Every April, Bhairav's giant chariot is pulled right through this square in a tug-of-war. Book a verified local storyteller nearby and let a guide tell you how Bisket Jatra works.

loreChunks.title: The Oldest Heart of Bhaktapur
loreChunks.text: Tachupal Square, where the Dattatreya temple stands, is the oldest part of Bhaktapur, and the temple is traditionally dated to 1427, during the reign of King Yaksha Malla, who ruled a unified Kathmandu Valley from Bhaktapur. Like Kasthamandap in Kathmandu, it is said to have been built from the timber of a single tree. The square was the original centre of the city before the royal palace and Durbar Square were developed further west, and it is surrounded by monastic residences known as maths, including the Pujari Math with its famous Peacock Window. Dattatreya is a deity revered by followers of Shiva and Vishnu and, in some traditions, by Buddhists, and his temple's long history reflects Bhaktapur's religious diversity. The square remains a quieter, more residential space than Durbar Square, popular with visitors who want to see everyday life.

loreChunks.title: A Pagoda with a Porch
loreChunks.text: The Dattatreya temple is a three-tiered pagoda raised on a plinth, distinguished by a projecting front section that forms a kind of porch, an unusual feature among Newar temples. Its stairway is guarded by statues of the wrestlers Jayamal and Phattu, the same legendary strongmen who appear at the base of Nyatapola. A pillar topped by a Garuda stands in front of the temple, and other statues and shrines fill the square. The temple's carved struts depict deities, and some lower carvings show erotic scenes. The combination of the porch and the three-tiered roofs gives the temple a distinctive silhouette that anchors the eastern end of Tachupal Square. Around it, the square is lined with traditional brick buildings, many of them maths and residences, which create a harmonious ensemble of Newar urban architecture.

loreChunks.title: Three Gods in One
loreChunks.text: Dattatreya is a composite deity who combines aspects of Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva, the creator, preserver and destroyer of the Hindu trinity. He is often depicted with three heads and six arms, carrying the emblems of each god, and accompanied by a cow and four dogs that are said to symbolise the Vedas. In some traditions he is regarded as a great yogi and teacher, and in Nepal he is honoured by many communities. The Garuda pillar in front of the temple reflects Vishnu's presence, while the trident emblems on the temple refer to Shiva. The wrestlers guarding the stairway link the temple with Nyatapola and the broader iconographic programme of Bhaktapur. This inclusive character makes Dattatreya a fitting deity for a square that has been the city's oldest meeting place for centuries, welcoming devotees of many traditions.

loreChunks.title: Pilgrims from Near and Far
loreChunks.text: The Dattatreya temple attracts worshippers from across Nepal and India, especially during festivals associated with the deity. Shivaratri, the great night of Shiva, brings large numbers of pilgrims, including sadhus who travel to the valley's sacred sites. Local residents worship daily at the temple and its surrounding shrines, and the square is a place of gathering where elders sit on temple plinths and children play. Bhaktapur's maths, the monastic residences around the square, were historically home to priests and ascetics, and some of them hosted pilgrims and religious teachers. The square's residential character and its surrounding workshops, including woodcarvers and potters, make it a place where religious and everyday life blend seamlessly. Visitors are welcome to observe worship and to explore the surrounding courtyards, many of which hold small shrines and carved details.

loreChunks.title: Tachupal's Survival
loreChunks.text: The Dattatreya temple survived the 1934 and 2015 earthquakes with damage that required repair but not complete rebuilding, while some surrounding buildings suffered more severely. Restoration after 2015 was carried out by Bhaktapur Municipality and partners, with traditional craftsmen repairing the timber struts, roofs and brickwork. Tachupal Square also benefited from the Bhaktapur Development Project of the 1970s and 1980s, supported by Germany, which restored many buildings and improved drainage and sanitation, helping to preserve the square's historic character. The project is remembered as a pioneering example of integrated urban conservation in Nepal. Today the square's maths, including the Pujari Math, house museums and community facilities. Visitors can support the square's conservation by respecting residents' privacy and by buying crafts from local workshops, which sustain traditional skills.

audioHook.script: Walk east to Tachupal, the oldest square in Bhaktapur, and you will meet two familiar faces. The stone wrestlers guarding this temple's stairs are Jayamal and Phattu, the same legendary strongmen who guard Nyatapola. This is the temple of Dattatreya, one god who combines Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva, and tradition says it was built in 1427 from the timber of a single tree, during the reign of King Yaksha Malla. Long before the royal palace grew up to the west, this square was the heart of the city. Today it is quieter, full of woodcarvers, potters and elders resting on temple steps. And just behind you hides one of the most famous windows in Nepal. Book a verified local storyteller nearby and let a guide lead you to the peacock.

loreChunks.title: A Priest's House and a Famous Window
loreChunks.text: The Pujari Math, a priests' residence on a lane beside Tachupal Square, is one of several maths that once housed priests and ascetics serving Bhaktapur's temples. The building in its present form dates largely from the eighteenth century, but its most famous feature, the Peacock Window, is often said to be older and is traditionally attributed to the fifteenth century. The math was associated with priests who served the Dattatreya temple, and it was a wealthy institution with lands and endowments. In the 1970s the building was restored with German assistance as part of the wider Bhaktapur conservation effort, reportedly as a gift linked to the wedding of Crown Prince Birendra, and it now houses the National Woodcarving Museum. The window has become a symbol of Newar craftsmanship, reproduced on postcards and in souvenir carvings sold throughout Nepal.

loreChunks.title: Latticework in Wood
loreChunks.text: The Peacock Window is a small latticed window set into the brick wall of the Pujari Math, on a narrow lane where visitors often gather to admire it. Its central panel shows a peacock with its tail fanned out in a circle of intricately carved feathers, surrounded by smaller birds, flowers and geometric patterns. The window's lattice was carved with such precision that the peacock seems to emerge from the frame. Newar window-carving is a demanding craft, requiring the joining of many separately carved pieces without nails, and the Peacock Window is considered one of its greatest achievements. Inside, the math's courtyard is lined with carved windows, struts and doors, many of which are also remarkable. The National Woodcarving Museum displays examples of carving from across the valley, offering useful context for the window outside in the lane.

loreChunks.title: The Peacock's Meaning
loreChunks.text: The peacock is a rich symbol in South Asian art. In Hindu mythology it is the vehicle of Kumar, the warrior son of Shiva and Parvati, and it is associated with beauty, immortality and the monsoon, since peacocks dance at the onset of the rains. In Buddhist imagery the peacock can symbolise the transformation of poison into wisdom, since peacocks were believed to eat poisonous plants without harm. The window's designers may have intended several of these meanings, and its placement on a priests' residence suggests a sacred purpose beyond decoration. The surrounding birds and flowers create an image of paradise, and the circular fan of the tail evokes a mandala. Visitors who look closely will find that each feather is carved individually, a testament to the patience of the craftsman who made it so many centuries ago.

loreChunks.title: The Living Craft of Woodcarving
loreChunks.text: The Peacock Window is not a site of worship, but it plays a role in Bhaktapur's living craft tradition. The city's woodcarvers, many of whom have workshops around Tachupal Square, learn their skills through apprenticeships within families, and they regard works like the Peacock Window as models of excellence. Reproductions of the window in various sizes are carved for sale to visitors, providing income for carvers and keeping the skills alive. The National Woodcarving Museum in the Pujari Math helps to explain the history and techniques of the craft. During festivals, the maths around the square host religious activities, and the area fills with music and processions. Visitors can watch carvers at work in nearby workshops and learn how traditional tools and techniques are used to create the intricate patterns that make Bhaktapur's woodwork famous across the world.

loreChunks.title: Protecting a Masterpiece
loreChunks.text: Wooden windows are vulnerable to rot, insects, sun and rain, and the Peacock Window's survival for centuries reflects both the quality of its timber and careful maintenance. The restoration of the Pujari Math in the 1970s included conservation of the window and the building's other carvings, and the building has been maintained since then as a museum. The 2015 earthquake damaged buildings around Tachupal Square, and the math required inspection and repair. Conservation of carved wood involves treating it against insects, consolidating weakened areas and ensuring that the surrounding walls protect it from water. Crowds of visitors who touch the window add to wear, so a protective approach is needed. Visitors can help by admiring the window without touching it, and by supporting the woodcarving museum and the local carvers whose work sustains the craft today.

audioHook.script: Turn down this narrow lane beside Tachupal Square and look for a small crowd staring at a wall. They are looking at the Peacock Window, perhaps the most famous window in Nepal. In its centre, a peacock spreads its tail in a perfect circle of carved feathers, each one shaped by hand, surrounded by birds and flowers. It belongs to the Pujari Math, an old house for temple priests, and tradition dates the window to the fifteenth century. In the 1970s the house was restored with German help and became a woodcarving museum. Now look around the lane: carvers in nearby workshops still learn by copying this very peacock. What does a peacock mean to a Hindu, and to a Buddhist? Book a verified local storyteller nearby and let a guide introduce you to the carvers.

loreChunks.title: The Last Malla King's Gift
loreChunks.text: The Golden Gate, known in Newar as Lu Dhowka, was completed in 1754 by King Ranajit Malla, the last Malla king of Bhaktapur. It forms the entrance to the inner courtyards of the palace, including Taleju Chowk, the shrine of the royal goddess. Ranajit Malla's reign was overshadowed by the rising power of Prithvi Narayan Shah of Gorkha, who would conquer Bhaktapur in 1769, and the gate is one of the last great works of the Malla dynasty. The British writer Perceval Landon, who wrote about Nepal in the early twentieth century, famously described it as the most lovely piece of art in the whole kingdom. Its creation shows that even in a period of political danger, Bhaktapur's rulers continued to invest in religious art of the highest quality, devoting resources to the goddess whose protection they sought.

loreChunks.title: Gilded Copper Repousse
loreChunks.text: The Golden Gate is made of gilded copper repousse, metal hammered from behind into high relief, mounted on a frame set into a whitewashed palace wall. Above the doorway rises a torana, a semicircular panel crowded with deities and mythical creatures, crowned by a figure of Garuda. The doorway's frame is decorated with images of gods, goddesses and guardians, and the whole composition glitters in sunlight. The gate stands at the junction between the public square and the private ritual world of the palace, and its splendour marks this transition. Repousse was a speciality of Newar metalworkers, who produced gilded gateways, roofs, banners and images for temples across the valley and in Tibet. The Golden Gate is among the finest examples of their art, and its craftsmanship can be appreciated in detail from close range by visitors standing in the square.

loreChunks.title: Taleju with Many Arms
loreChunks.text: The central figure of the torana above the Golden Gate is a multi-armed form of the goddess Taleju, the royal deity of the Malla kings, often identified with a form of Durga. She is shown with many arms holding weapons and attributes, and she is surrounded by attendant deities and protective figures. At the top of the torana, Garuda, the bird-mount of Vishnu, grasps serpents in his hands, a common motif in Newar toranas. Makaras, mythical water creatures, and other figures fill the frame. The gate's iconography announces that the courtyards beyond are under the goddess's protection and that entry requires respect and purity. For the king it was a declaration that his palace and power were sustained by the goddess. Visitors can stand before the gate and identify individual figures, many of which retain remarkable detail after more than 250 years.

loreChunks.title: Gateway to Taleju Chowk
loreChunks.text: The Golden Gate leads toward Taleju Chowk, the courtyard of the royal goddess, which is closed to non-Hindus. During Dashain, Taleju receives special rituals, and the gate becomes the threshold of the year's most important ceremonies in the palace, including sacrifices offered by priests. On ordinary days the gate is guarded, and visitors may pass through it to reach parts of the palace that are open, such as the courtyard with the Naga Pokhari bath, while respecting the restricted areas beyond. The gate is also a gathering point for visitors and photographers in the square, and its gilded surface catches the light of the morning sun. Its role as a boundary between public and sacred space continues to be observed, and visitors should follow the guidance of guards and signs regarding which areas they may enter and photograph.

loreChunks.title: Keeping the Gold Bright
loreChunks.text: Gilded copper is durable, but it is vulnerable to pollution, moisture and handling, which can dull the gilding and corrode the metal beneath. The Golden Gate has been cleaned and conserved at various times, and its setting in the palace wall was damaged in the 1934 and 2015 earthquakes, requiring repair of the surrounding masonry. Conservation of the gate is a specialised task involving metal conservators, who clean the surface carefully, stabilise any corrosion and, where appropriate, renew the gilding using traditional techniques. Bhaktapur Municipality and the Department of Archaeology oversee such work. Because the gate is a ritual threshold, conservation must also be coordinated with the priests of Taleju. Visitors can help preserve the gate by not touching its surface, as oils from hands accelerate tarnishing, and by supporting the city's heritage fees.

audioHook.script: Stop in front of this glittering doorway set into a white palace wall. A British writer a century ago called it the most lovely piece of art in the whole kingdom. This is the Golden Gate, made of gilded copper hammered into relief, and it was completed in 1754 by King Ranajit Malla, the last Malla king of Bhaktapur, only fifteen years before he lost his kingdom. Look up at the arch above the door: a many-armed goddess, Taleju, the royal protector, surrounded by guardians, with Garuda at the top gripping serpents in his hands. Beyond this gate lies the goddess's courtyard, closed to all but Hindu worshippers. How many weapons is she holding? loreChunks.title: The Builder King in Bronze
loreChunks.text: The gilt-bronze statue of King Bhupatindra Malla, seated atop a stone column in Bhaktapur Durbar Square, honours the ruler who shaped much of the city's present appearance. Bhupatindra reigned from 1696 to 1722 and commissioned Nyatapola, remodelled the Fifty-Five Window Palace and raised the Bhairavnath temple to three tiers. His statue was set up facing the palace and the courtyard of Taleju, so that the king would remain in perpetual devotion before the royal goddess. The column follows a custom shared with Kathmandu and Patan, where similar statues of kings stand before their palaces. Bhupatindra's reputation as a patron of the arts is reflected in the quality of the statue itself, which many consider one of the finest royal portraits in the valley, and in the many legends about his personal involvement in building projects across the city.

loreChunks.title: A King on a Column
loreChunks.text: The statue sits on a lotus-shaped base at the top of a tall stone column, raising the king above the crowds in the square. The column stands on a stepped plinth, and its placement in front of the palace aligns the king's gaze with the Golden Gate and the courtyards beyond. The gilt-bronze figure is finely cast, with detailed jewellery, clothing and facial features, and it shows the king seated with his hands folded in a gesture of devotion. Unlike Patan's Yoganarendra Malla, who kneels beneath a cobra hood, Bhupatindra is shown without a canopy, giving his statue a simpler, more direct presence. The column itself is slender and plain, focusing attention on the figure above. Viewed from the square, the king appears framed against the palace, uniting the ruler, his residence and his goddess in a single view.

loreChunks.title: Devotion Made Permanent
loreChunks.text: The king's folded hands express devotion to the goddess Taleju, whose courtyard lies beyond the Golden Gate. By placing his image in this posture before her shrine, Bhupatindra ensured that his worship would continue forever, even after his death. The statue therefore functions as both a portrait and a perpetual offering. Royal statues of this kind also asserted the king's legitimacy, showing him as the goddess's chosen servant. In the Malla cities, kings identified closely with their deities, and their images appear in temple carvings and paintings as well as on columns. Another statue of Bhupatindra and his queen, kneeling inside a cage, stands in the courtyard of Changu Narayan, a reminder of the king's devotion to Vishnu as well as to the goddess. Comparing the two statues reveals different aspects of royal piety in Malla Bhaktapur.

loreChunks.title: A King Who Still Watches
loreChunks.text: The statue does not receive formal worship, but it remains a respected presence in the square. During festivals, when processions and masked dances fill Bhaktapur Durbar Square, the king appears to watch from his column, as he once watched from the palace windows. Residents tell stories about Bhupatindra's building projects, including the tale that he carried bricks himself during the construction of Nyatapola to encourage his subjects. Such stories emphasise the king's personal involvement in the city's sacred works and his close relationship with its people. For visitors, the statue offers a way to connect the monuments of Bhaktapur with the individual who commissioned many of them. A guide can explain how the king's projects transformed the city, and how his legacy continues to shape Bhaktapur's sense of identity and pride.

loreChunks.title: Survival Through Earthquakes
loreChunks.text: The column and statue survived the 1934 and 2015 earthquakes, although the square around them suffered heavy damage. After 2015 the column was inspected for stability and the statue for any loosening from its base. Gilt-bronze requires periodic cleaning and conservation of its surface, which can be damaged by pollution, bird droppings and weathering. Such work requires scaffolding and specialist conservators and is coordinated by Bhaktapur Municipality and the Department of Archaeology. The statue's height protects it from handling, but it also makes it harder to inspect, so detailed photographs taken with zoom lenses are useful for monitoring its condition. Saalik's field collectors are asked to capture close-up images of the statue's face, hands and base, contributing to a record that conservators can use to track any changes over time.

audioHook.script: High on a stone column in front of the palace sits a golden king with his hands folded in prayer. Meet Bhupatindra Malla, the builder king of Bhaktapur, who ruled from 1696 to 1722. Almost everything you have admired here carries his mark: he raised Nyatapola, remodelled the Fifty-Five Window Palace and gave the Bhairav temple its three roofs. Legend says he even carried bricks himself to inspire his people. His statue faces the Golden Gate and the courtyard of the royal goddess, so that his devotion would never end. And at Changu Narayan, up the hill, the same king kneels again, this time inside a cage. Why a cage? loreChunks.title: The Great Pond at the City Gate
loreChunks.text: Siddha Pokhari is a large rectangular pond near the western entrance to Bhaktapur's old city, traditionally attributed to the fifteenth century and the reign of King Yaksha Malla. Ponds like this were essential to Newar towns: they stored rainwater, recharged the groundwater that fed the city's stone spouts, supplied water for irrigation and firefighting, and provided places for ritual bathing. Siddha Pokhari, also known as Ta Pukhu, the great pond, is one of the largest in Bhaktapur, and its position at the city's edge made it a landmark for travellers arriving from Kathmandu. Over the centuries its banks have been lined with shrines, statues and resting places. Today the pond is a popular place for residents to walk, meet and feed the fish, and its open space contrasts with the dense streets of the old city beyond.

loreChunks.title: Engineering Water for a City
loreChunks.text: Siddha Pokhari is a carefully engineered reservoir with stone and brick embankments, walkways and steps leading down to the water. Ponds in the Kathmandu Valley were connected to networks of canals and underground channels that distributed water to spouts and fields, and Siddha Pokhari played a role in this system for Bhaktapur. Its large surface area allowed it to collect monsoon rain and hold it through the dry season, while seepage from the pond recharged aquifers. The banks are punctuated by small shrines and statues, and the walkways invite circulation around the water. The pond's rectangular shape and scale give it a monumental quality, and from its banks visitors can see the roofs of Bhaktapur rising beyond. Restoration work has aimed to improve water quality and reinforce the embankments against erosion and earthquake damage.

loreChunks.title: The Serpent in the Pond
loreChunks.text: Like many ponds in the valley, Siddha Pokhari is the subject of legends involving serpents and tantric power. One widely told story says that a giant serpent lives at the bottom of the pond. In another, a tantric attempted to defeat the serpent by transforming himself into a snake, asking his wife to sprinkle him with consecrated rice to restore his human form. Frightened by his transformation, she fled, and he remained a serpent in the pond forever. These legends connect the pond with the nagas, the serpent spirits believed to control water, and with the tantric traditions that are strong in Bhaktapur. Small shrines around the banks honour deities associated with water and protection. Visitors who sit by the pond in the evening may hear residents tell their own versions of the story, which remains part of the city's folklore.

loreChunks.title: Bathing, Feeding Fish and Evening Walks
loreChunks.text: Siddha Pokhari has long been a place of ritual and recreation. Residents have bathed in its water on auspicious days, and the pond's shrines receive offerings. Feeding the fish is a popular activity, believed to earn merit, and children and families gather on the banks to throw grains into the water. In the evenings the pond becomes a social space, where people walk, sit and talk as the sun sets over the hills to the west. During some festivals the banks host gatherings and rituals. The pond also had practical importance: in the past it supplied water for the city and its fields, and it remains part of Bhaktapur's water landscape. Visitors arriving by bus or taxi often pass the pond on their way into the old city, and it makes a pleasant place to begin or end a day of exploring Bhaktapur on foot.

loreChunks.title: Restoring a Traditional Reservoir
loreChunks.text: Ponds like Siddha Pokhari face threats from pollution, siltation, encroachment and changes in the water table. Over the decades the pond's water quality declined and its embankments weakened, and the 2015 earthquake added further stress. Bhaktapur Municipality has undertaken restoration work, including dredging, reinforcement of the banks and efforts to improve the water supply and quality. Such projects aim to restore the pond's ecological and hydrological functions as well as its appearance, recognising that traditional ponds are part of a sustainable water management system. Community involvement has been important, with residents taking part in cleaning campaigns and festivals that celebrate the pond. Visitors can help by not littering and by respecting the pond's role in the city's life. Its revival is part of a broader movement in the valley to restore traditional water systems.

audioHook.script: Before you walk into old Bhaktapur, pause beside this great rectangular pond. Siddha Pokhari, also called the great pond, has stored the city's rainwater since around the fifteenth century, feeding its stone spouts and fields. But residents will tell you something else lives here. Legend says a tantric once turned himself into a serpent to fight a monster in the pond, and asked his wife to sprinkle him with blessed rice to change him back. She was too frightened, ran away, and he has been a snake beneath these waters ever since. Today families feed the fish here and stroll the banks at sunset. Is the serpent still down there? loreChunks.title: A Pilgrim Road to Vishnu
loreChunks.text: For centuries, pilgrims have walked from Bhaktapur to the hilltop temple of Changu Narayan, the oldest Vishnu temple in the valley, about six kilometres to the north. The route crosses farmland north of the city and climbs a forested ridge to the temple, which sits on a hill overlooking the eastern valley. Before roads and buses, this path was the main way for Bhaktapur's residents to reach Changu Narayan for festivals and vows, and pilgrims from across the valley followed it as well. The trail is now popular with walkers seeking a quieter alternative to the busy heritage squares, offering a glimpse of rural Newar life. Its starting points on the northern edge of Bhaktapur, near temples such as Kamal Binayak, connect the city's sacred geography with that of the surrounding countryside and its hill shrines.

loreChunks.title: Villages, Terraces and Wayside Shrines
loreChunks.text: The trail's architecture is that of the rural valley: terraced rice and vegetable fields, brick farmhouses, small Newar villages and wayside shrines. Along the way, walkers pass shrines to Ganesh, small chaityas and resting platforms called patis, where pilgrims and farmers could shelter from sun and rain. The village architecture follows the same principles as Bhaktapur's urban buildings, with brick walls, carved windows and tiled roofs, but on a humbler scale. As the trail climbs toward Changu, the landscape opens up, offering views over the valley and, on clear days, of the Himalayan peaks to the north. The final approach passes through the village of Changu, with its traditional houses and shops lining the stone-paved path to the temple courtyard. The walk thus offers a continuous experience of Newar settlement from city to village to hilltop.

loreChunks.title: Ganesh at the Start, Vishnu at the End
loreChunks.text: Pilgrimage routes in the Kathmandu Valley are marked by shrines that structure the journey. Ganesh, the remover of obstacles, is often worshipped at the start of a journey, and shrines to him appear at trailheads and crossroads. Along the route, small chaityas and images of local deities offer places for prayer. At the end of the trail, Changu Narayan, one of the most important Vishnu temples in Nepal, awaits with its extraordinary collection of Licchavi sculptures, including images of Vishnu riding Garuda and the cosmic form of Vishnu. The journey from Ganesh to Vishnu expresses a progression from overcoming obstacles to reaching the preserver of the universe. For pilgrims, walking the trail is part of the act of devotion, and the effort of the climb adds merit. Walkers today can follow this symbolic path while enjoying the countryside.

loreChunks.title: Walking for Festivals and Vows
loreChunks.text: Pilgrims walk to Changu Narayan for festivals, especially on Ekadashi days sacred to Vishnu and during the month of Kartik, when Vishnu worship is particularly important. Some devotees make the journey to fulfil vows, walking barefoot or carrying offerings. In the past, groups from Bhaktapur's neighbourhoods would walk together, singing devotional songs along the way. Farmers along the route have their own rituals connected with planting and harvest, and walkers may encounter these in season, such as the rice-planting festivities of the monsoon. The trail also serves daily needs, connecting villages with the city's markets. Visitors who walk the route should carry water, wear sturdy shoes and start early to avoid the midday heat. Hiring a local guide helps to navigate the network of paths and to understand the villages and shrines along the way.

loreChunks.title: Rural Heritage After 2015
loreChunks.text: The 2015 earthquake caused severe damage in the villages between Bhaktapur and Changu Narayan, destroying many traditional houses and damaging shrines and resting places. Reconstruction has been uneven: some households rebuilt in traditional styles with support from heritage programmes, while others turned to concrete, changing the character of the villages. Changu Narayan's temple complex was also damaged and has been restored. The trail itself faces pressure from road building and urban expansion as Bhaktapur's suburbs spread northward into farmland. Preserving the route as a walking path, with its shrines and views, requires coordination between municipalities, communities and tourism organisations. Responsible tourism can help by bringing income to village homestays and cafes. Saalik's field collectors document wayside shrines along the route, adding small heritage sites that are often overlooked in conservation planning.

audioHook.script: From here, an old pilgrim road leaves Bhaktapur and climbs north through rice terraces and brick villages to a hilltop temple about six kilometres away. That temple, Changu Narayan, is the oldest Vishnu temple in the valley, with sculptures carved some fifteen hundred years ago. Before buses, this was how Bhaktapur's families reached it, walking together and singing on festival mornings. Start, as pilgrims do, by greeting Ganesh, the remover of obstacles, and watch for small shrines and resting platforms along the way. On clear days the Himalaya appears over the ridge. The trail forks often, and village paths change after every monsoon. Want to arrive at Changu without getting lost? loreChunks.title: A Neighbourhood Temple of Vishnu
loreChunks.text: Wakupati Narayan is a temple of Vishnu in eastern Bhaktapur, near Tachupal Square, in one of the city's older residential neighbourhoods. Its precise founding date has not been firmly established in the published sources available to Saalik, and it is attributed on stylistic grounds to the Malla period, when Bhaktapur's neighbourhoods built temples to their protective deities. Vishnu, worshipped here as Narayan, was an important deity in Malla Bhaktapur, alongside the royal goddess Taleju and the city's many forms of Bhairav and the mother goddesses. Neighbourhood temples like Wakupati Narayan were maintained by local guthis, trusts of families who shared responsibility for rituals and upkeep, and many of these institutions continue today. The temple offers visitors a sense of how Bhaktapur's sacred life extends far beyond Durbar Square into every quarter of the city.

loreChunks.title: Gilded Roofs in a Quiet Square
loreChunks.text: Wakupati Narayan is a two-tiered pagoda with gilded metal elements on its roofs, which give it a bright appearance unusual for a neighbourhood temple. In front of the temple stand pillars topped by figures of Garuda, Vishnu's bird-mount, a common feature of Vishnu temples. The temple's struts and doors are carved with deities and decorative motifs, and the plinth provides a place for residents to sit. The square around it is lined with traditional brick houses with carved windows, creating an intimate setting quite different from the grand public spaces of Durbar Square and Taumadhi. The temple's scale and decoration reflect the wealth and devotion of the neighbourhood that sponsored it. Visitors can appreciate the craftsmanship of the struts and the gilded elements at close range, often without the crowds that gather at the more famous monuments.

loreChunks.title: Narayan and Garuda
loreChunks.text: Narayan, the form of Vishnu worshipped at this temple, is the preserver of the cosmic order, and his iconography includes the conch, discus, mace and lotus, which he holds in his four hands. Garuda, the eagle-like bird who carries Vishnu, appears on the pillars in front of the temple, kneeling in devotion. The combination of the temple and its Garuda pillars is characteristic of Vishnu shrines across the valley, from the great temple of Changu Narayan to the smaller neighbourhood temples of the cities. The struts of the temple depict Vishnu's avatars and attendants, as well as other deities. For neighbourhood residents, Narayan is a protector who ensures prosperity and harmony. The temple's iconography thus links the local community with the great mythology of Vishnu and with the network of Vishnu temples spread across the Kathmandu Valley.

loreChunks.title: Ekadashi and Neighbourhood Festivals
loreChunks.text: Wakupati Narayan receives daily worship from residents, and Ekadashi, the eleventh day of each lunar fortnight, brings additional devotees, since it is sacred to Vishnu. During the month of Kartik, Vishnu worship intensifies, with lamps lit and special rituals performed. The temple's guthi organises festivals and maintains the rituals, and neighbourhood residents take part in feasts and processions on important days. Bhaktapur's festival calendar is rich, and neighbourhood temples like Wakupati Narayan play a role in city-wide celebrations as well as local ones. During Bisket Jatra and other festivals, processions may pass through the area. Visitors who wander into the square may find residents making offerings, children playing and elders chatting on the plinth, a scene of everyday devotion that reveals the continuing importance of neighbourhood temples in Bhaktapur's life.

loreChunks.title: Caring for Neighbourhood Heritage
loreChunks.text: Neighbourhood temples like Wakupati Narayan depend on local guthis and residents for their maintenance, often with support from Bhaktapur Municipality. The 2015 earthquake damaged many temples and houses in Bhaktapur's neighbourhoods, and restoration of smaller temples sometimes lagged behind work on the famous monuments. Bhaktapur Municipality's heritage programme, funded partly by visitor fees, has supported the restoration of neighbourhood temples, and community groups have raised funds for repairs. Conservation involves repairing timber and brickwork, maintaining roofs and conserving gilded elements. The challenge is to sustain the guthi system, which has been weakened by social change and by land reforms that reduced guthi income. Visitors who explore neighbourhoods like this one contribute to their economic life, and documenting such temples helps ensure they are not overlooked in heritage planning.

audioHook.script: Wander a few lanes away from the crowds, and you will find this two-roofed temple glinting with gold in a quiet square. Wakupati Narayan is a neighbourhood temple of Vishnu, and the stone birds kneeling on the pillars in front of it are Garudas, Vishnu's mounts. No royal founder is recorded in Saalik's sources, and the temple's exact age is still being researched. What makes it special is the neighbourhood itself: the families whose trust has kept this temple alive for generations, the elders on the plinth and the children playing in the square. This is how most of Bhaktapur actually worships. How does a neighbourhood guthi work, and who pays for the gold? loreChunks.title: The Kings' Serpent Bath
loreChunks.text: Naga Pokhari is a royal bath tank within the Bhaktapur palace complex, reached through the Golden Gate. It is usually attributed to the seventeenth century, and some accounts associate it with King Jitamitra Malla, who reigned in the later part of that century. The tank was used by the royal family for ritual bathing, particularly by those preparing for worship of Taleju, the royal goddess whose shrine lies nearby. Its name, 'serpent pond', refers to the stone nagas that decorate it. Like the royal baths of Kathmandu and Patan, Naga Pokhari expresses the close connection between water, purity and kingship in Malla culture. After the Shah conquest the palace lost its royal function, but the bath remained, and it is now one of the features visitors can see inside the palace complex, beyond the gilded gate that faces the square.

loreChunks.title: Stone, Water and Serpents
loreChunks.text: Naga Pokhari is a rectangular tank lined with stone, with steps leading down to the water and a gilded spout through which water enters. At the centre of the tank rises a stone column topped by a naga, a serpent spirit, its hood raised above the water. Smaller serpents are carved around the tank's rim. The water was supplied through channels from the surrounding hills, part of the network that fed the city's spouts and ponds. The tank's design is simple compared with the elaborately carved Tusha Hiti in Patan, but its proportions and the dramatic central serpent give it a powerful presence. It is set within a courtyard of the palace, enclosed by walls, creating a private space for royal ritual. The combination of stone, water and the gilded spout reflects the importance of water in Newar ritual architecture.

loreChunks.title: Nagas, Guardians of Water
loreChunks.text: Nagas are serpent spirits who play a central role in the mythology of the Kathmandu Valley. Legend tells that the valley was once a lake inhabited by nagas, and that when the lake was drained, the nagas remained as guardians of water and rain. Their worship is considered essential for ensuring the monsoon, and they are honoured at ponds, springs and spouts across the valley, especially during the festival of Nag Panchami. The naga rising from the centre of Naga Pokhari embodies this power, ensuring that the royal bath was supplied with pure water and that the king's ritual purity was protected. The serpents around the rim reinforce this protection, and the gilded spout adds the dimension of royal splendour. For visitors, the bath offers a glimpse of how the valley's mythology of water was expressed in royal architecture.

loreChunks.title: Purification Before Worship
loreChunks.text: Royal bathing at Naga Pokhari was a ritual act, part of the preparations for worshipping Taleju and for performing other ceremonies. Bathing in water protected by the nagas purified the body and mind, allowing the king or members of the royal family to approach the goddess. Such rituals reflected the Malla kings' role as sacred rulers whose ritual purity was linked with the kingdom's well-being. Today the bath is no longer used for royal ritual, but it remains a reminder of these practices. During Nag Panchami, when nagas are honoured throughout the valley with pictures of serpents pasted above doorways, the significance of the bath's serpent imagery comes to the fore. Visitors to the palace complex can view the bath, but should respect its historical and religious significance and should never throw coins or other objects into the water.

loreChunks.title: Keeping the Royal Bath Intact
loreChunks.text: Naga Pokhari's conservation requires attention to both its stonework and its water supply. Stone tanks can crack in earthquakes, and the 1934 and 2015 earthquakes both damaged the Bhaktapur palace complex. The bath's water supply depends on channels that may have been disrupted by changes in the surrounding urban landscape. Conservation work by the Department of Archaeology and Bhaktapur Municipality has included repairs to the palace's courtyards and baths. Maintaining clean water in the tank is also a challenge, as stagnant water encourages algae that can damage stone surfaces. The naga column, as a slender element, must be monitored for stability. Visitors can help preserve the bath by not touching or climbing on its stonework and by supporting the city's heritage programme through the entry fee, which contributes to the upkeep of the whole palace complex.

audioHook.script: Pass through the Golden Gate into the palace and you will find a quiet stone tank with a serpent rising from the middle of the water. This is Naga Pokhari, the serpent pond, where Bhaktapur's royal family bathed before worshipping their goddess Taleju. Legend says the whole Kathmandu Valley was once a lake ruled by serpent spirits called nagas, and they still guard every spring, pond and spout. Here, the naga raises its hood above the water to keep the royal bath pure. Look around the rim for its smaller serpent companions, and at the golden spout where the water enters. Who drained the ancient lake, and why did the nagas stay? Book a verified local storyteller nearby and let a guide tell you the valley's oldest legend.

loreChunks.title: The Goddess's Courtyard
loreChunks.text: Taleju Chowk is the courtyard of the royal goddess Taleju within the Bhaktapur palace, reached through the Golden Gate. It is the most sacred space in the palace complex and has been closed to non-Hindus for centuries. The cult of Taleju, the tutelary goddess of the Malla kings, was central to royal power in Bhaktapur, as in Kathmandu and Patan, and the courtyard was the setting for the most important royal rituals. The palace's Taleju shrine was developed and embellished by successive Malla kings, including Bhupatindra and Ranajit Malla, who added the Golden Gate in 1754 as its grand approach. After the conquest of Bhaktapur in 1769, the shrine continued to function under its priests, and the Shah kings maintained Taleju's worship. The courtyard remains an active ritual space, guarded and protected from public access.

loreChunks.title: An Inner Sanctum of Carving
loreChunks.text: Because Taleju Chowk is closed to non-Hindus, most visitors know it only from descriptions and photographs. Published accounts describe a courtyard of exceptional richness, with carved and painted struts, doors and windows, gilded metalwork and shrines surrounding the central space. The courtyard follows the Newar quadrangle plan, enclosed by palace wings, with the shrine of Taleju forming its focus. The Golden Gate, which faces the public square, is the outer expression of this hidden splendour, and the quality of its craftsmanship hints at what lies beyond. Adjacent courtyards, including the one containing the Naga Pokhari bath, belong to the same complex. The separation between the public square and the inner courtyards reflects the layered structure of Newar palaces, in which access became more restricted the closer one moved to the sacred centre.

loreChunks.title: Taleju, Protector of Kings
loreChunks.text: Taleju is understood as a form of Durga, the warrior goddess, and she is closely associated with Tantric traditions. In Bhaktapur, as in the other Malla cities, her image is hidden from public view and served only by initiated priests. The courtyard's carvings, as described by those who have seen them, depict forms of the goddess, protective deities and attendants, creating a sacred enclosure around her shrine. The torana above the Golden Gate, with its multi-armed goddess, offers the public a glimpse of her iconography. Taleju's role as the protector of kings meant that her favour was essential to the kingdom's survival, and the rituals performed in her courtyard were believed to secure victory and prosperity. Her continued worship long after the end of the Malla kings shows the depth of her place in the religious life of Bhaktapur.

loreChunks.title: Dashain in Taleju Chowk
loreChunks.text: Taleju Chowk becomes the focus of Bhaktapur's most important royal rituals during Dashain, the autumn festival of the goddess Durga. Sacrifices are offered to Taleju by her priests, and the courtyard is the setting for ceremonies that once confirmed the king's protection for the coming year. Bhaktapur's Dashain celebrations are particularly rich, with masked dances, processions and rituals across the city. The Navadurga, the nine forms of the goddess, are embodied by masked dancers from a hereditary group who perform throughout the year in a cycle closely tied to the festival calendar. Although non-Hindus cannot enter the courtyard, they can observe some of the celebrations in the square outside. Visitors should respect the restrictions at the Golden Gate and follow the guidance of the guards, who protect the sanctity of the space for its worshippers.

loreChunks.title: Conserving a Restricted Space
loreChunks.text: Conservation of Taleju Chowk presents special challenges because of its restricted access and active ritual use. Work must be coordinated with priests and carried out by craftsmen who are permitted to enter, and documentation is limited by rules about photography. The 1934 and 2015 earthquakes damaged the palace complex, and the courtyard required repairs to its brickwork, timber and roofs. The Department of Archaeology and Bhaktapur Municipality oversee conservation in the palace, working with the religious authorities. The courtyard's carvings, considered among the finest in the valley by those who have seen them, require careful maintenance to protect them from weathering and insects. Saalik's field collectors do not enter or photograph restricted areas, so documentation of Taleju Chowk relies on permitted exterior views and on records held by the authorities.

audioHook.script: Stand at the Golden Gate and look through, as far as you are allowed. Beyond lies Taleju Chowk, the courtyard of the royal goddess of Bhaktapur, and for centuries no one but Hindu worshippers and her priests has stepped inside. Those who have describe carved and painted struts, gilded doors and shrines of extraordinary richness, all arranged around the hidden goddess who protected the Malla kings. Every Dashain her priests still perform sacrifices here, and masked dancers of the nine Durgas perform across the city. The Golden Gate in front of you is the public face of all that hidden splendour. What happens inside during Dashain night? Book a verified local storyteller nearby and let a guide who knows the rituals tell you what you cannot see.

loreChunks.title: Centuries of Clay
loreChunks.text: Pottery Square, known in Newar as Talako, lies a short walk south of Taumadhi Square in Bhaktapur and is home to the city's community of potters, the Prajapati, who have worked clay here for many generations. Bhaktapur's pottery tradition is often described as centuries old, supplying the valley with water jars, cooking pots, oil lamps, flower pots and ritual vessels used in festivals and household worship. The square's buildings were badly damaged in the 1934 earthquake and again in 2015, and many have been rebuilt, but the craft continues in the open spaces where pots are shaped, dried and fired. Saalik's sources do not record a founding date for the square itself, which developed organically as a craft neighbourhood. For visitors, the square offers a rare chance to see a traditional Newar craft practised in the same place and in much the same way as it has been for centuries.

loreChunks.title: A Workshop Under the Sky
loreChunks.text: Pottery Square is less a monument than a working landscape. Its open paving is covered with rows of freshly shaped pots drying in the sun, while potters sit at wheels under awnings or in doorways, spinning clay into vessels with practised speed. Around the square, brick houses with carved windows provide homes and storage, and kilns, traditionally built as mounds of straw and ash over stacked pots, are fired in corners of the square. A small shrine to Ganesh stands among the workshops, honoured by the potters before they begin work. The square's appearance changes through the day and the seasons, as pots are made, dried, fired and sold. Field collectors are asked to photograph the square at several times of day, recording the arrangement of drying pots, wheels and kilns, which are as much a part of its heritage as its buildings.

loreChunks.title: Ganesh and the Potter's Wheel
loreChunks.text: For the potters of Bhaktapur, clay is not only a material but part of a sacred cycle. Ritual vessels made here are used in temples and homes for offerings of water, milk and grain, and oil lamps light shrines across the city during festivals such as Tihar. The potters honour Ganesh, the remover of obstacles, at the small shrine in the square before beginning work and before firing their kilns, asking for success and protection from cracks and breakage. In Hindu thought, the potter shaping clay on the wheel is a powerful image of creation, used in scriptures to describe the divine shaping the world. The repeated forms of the pots drying in the square have their own beauty, recalling the repetition of images in temple carvings. For visitors, the square shows how sacred and everyday life are bound together in Newar craft traditions.

loreChunks.title: Lamps for Tihar, Jars for Weddings
loreChunks.text: Demand for pottery follows Bhaktapur's festival calendar. Before Tihar, the festival of lights in autumn, potters produce thousands of small oil lamps used to illuminate homes and temples. Weddings, funerals and other rites require specific vessels, some made only by particular families. The potters also make toys, figurines and decorative pieces for visitors, and many offer short lessons at the wheel, a popular activity that provides income for families. The square comes alive in the dry season, when pots can be dried in the sun, and quietens during the monsoon, when rain makes work difficult. Visitors are welcome to watch and buy, but should be careful not to step on drying pots and should ask before photographing people at work. A guide can arrange a pottery lesson and explain the techniques and rituals of the craft in detail.

loreChunks.title: Sustaining a Living Craft
loreChunks.text: Conserving Pottery Square means sustaining both its buildings and its craft. The 2015 earthquake damaged houses and workshops around the square, and families rebuilt with varying support, sometimes in traditional styles and sometimes with concrete. The craft itself faces pressures from cheap plastic and metal alternatives, from rising costs and from young people choosing other careers. Tourism has provided a new market for pottery and lessons, helping some families to continue, and Bhaktapur Municipality's heritage programme recognises the importance of living crafts alongside monuments. Air quality concerns about traditional open firing have prompted experiments with improved kilns. Documentation of the potters' techniques, tools, products and oral histories is as valuable as documenting the buildings. Saalik's field collectors are asked to record the square's activities and interview potters, with their consent, about the craft's past and future.

audioHook.script: Follow the lanes south from Taumadhi Square until the ground in front of you is covered with rows of clay pots drying in the sun. Welcome to Pottery Square, where Bhaktapur's potters have shaped clay for generations. Watch a potter set the wheel spinning and pull a water jar out of a lump of earth in less than a minute. Before work begins, the potters honour Ganesh at the little shrine here, asking him to keep their pots from cracking in the kiln. Before Tihar, the festival of lights, this square produces thousands of tiny oil lamps for the whole city. Many families here offer a short lesson at the wheel. Want to try? Watch your step around the drying pots. Book a verified local storyteller nearby and let a guide introduce you to a potter's family.
